newsitem.title: USA: Republicans, White House reach some budget agreements.
newsitem.headline: Republicans, White House reach some budget agreements.

text.p: Congressional Republicans Friday tentatively agreed to a White House demand to restore federal disability benefits to legal immigrants, as the two sides moved closer to a deal on balanced-budget legislation.
Republican leaders and the White House negotiated throughout the day, trying to work out a final deal on spending and tax legislation needed to implement a five-year balanced-budget deal.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici said only about six or seven spending items remained open and that the two sides hoped to finish work Friday night. The outlook for the tax bill was less clear.

Aides said remaining issues included the structure of a new children's health programme and its funding level, and labour protections for welfare recipients in workfare programmes. They cautioned no agreements were final until the deal was done.

Republicans have agreed to provide at least $16 billion for a new initiative to cover many of the nation's 10 million uninsured children. The White House is pushing for an additional $8 billion, which was provided by the Senate as part of a 20-cents-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax.
"I think we're going to get this agreement," Clinton told an education group earlier Friday, after discussing the negotiations with top aides.

A welfare reform law that took effect last year eliminates most federal benefits to legal immigrants this fall. Clinton has been pushing to partially restore such aid, but Republicans had initially taken a hard line.

Congressional aides said Republican leaders came around to the White House position Friday, agreeing to continue Supplemental Security Income (SSI) disability benefits to all legal immigrants on the rolls as of Aug. 22, 1996, when the welfare bill was signed. That would affect about 500,000 immigrants.
In addition, immigrants in the country on that date who became disabled in the future would be eligible for aid.

Republicans also dropped a plan, opposed by the White House, that would have let states reduce special supplemental payments to elderly individuals receiving disability benefits. They also agreed to an administration demand to continue Medicaid benefits to children who lose SSI benefits under the welfare law.

Republicans have set Aug. 1 as the deadline for passing final tax and spending bills to implement a five-year balanced budget pact with the White House. After that date, Congress is scheduled to adjourn for a month-long recess.
The tax bill would reduce revenues by $85 billion over five years. The spending measure includes $115 billion in Medicare reductions and about $15 billion in Medicaid cuts.
Congressional Republicans sped up the budget talks, some Democrats tried to apply the brakes warning President Clinton not to rush into a final deal.

Led by New York Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, Democrats on the influential Senate Finance Committee asked Clinton to defer final action until the fall if necessary in order to work out legislation that met party priorities.

They predicted the federal budget deficit could shrink to about $30 billion at the close of fiscal 1997, which ends Sept. 30. If current trends continued, the budget could be in balance next year without new action by Congress.
Republican lawmakers warned delay would only make it harder to get a final deal.
"If there are differences, they are going to remain in September and the chances of passing (the budget bill) will be greatly diminished," Domenici said.

Among major disagreements on the tax bill, the White House opposes a Republican tax plan indexing capital gains for inflation. Administration officials are also pushing to extend a $500-per-child tax credit to low-income workers.
